concepts.def: A microorganism that causes infectious disease. Pathogens may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi. They may infect plants or animals and can be spread by direct contact, by water or by air.

concepts.term: rapid reproduction of pathogens in the body
concepts.def: Bacteria and viruses may reproduce rapidly inside the body, so the number of pathogens present can rise quickly after an infection begins.
A poison that bacteria may produce. Toxins damage tissues and make us feel ill.
Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage. This is how a viral infection harms the body, rather than by producing toxins.

A viral disease showing symptoms of fever and a red skin rash. The measles virus is spread by inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs. Measles is a serious illness that can be fatal if complications arise, and for this reason most young children are vaccinated against measles.

HIV is a virus that initially causes a flu-like illness and is spread by sexual contact or exchange of body fluids such as blood, which occurs when drug users share needles. Unless successfully controlled with antiretroviral drugs the virus attacks the body's immune cells. Late stage HIV infection, or AIDS, occurs when the body's immune system becomes so badly damaged it can no longer deal with other infections or cancers.

A widespread plant pathogen affecting many species of plants including tomatoes. It gives a distinctive 'mosaic' pattern of discolouration on the leaves which affects the growth of the plant due to lack of photosynthesis.

A bacterial disease spread by bacteria ingested in food, or on food prepared in unhygienic conditions. Fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea are caused by the bacteria and the toxins they secrete. In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.

A sexually transmitted disease (STD) caused by a bacterium, with symptoms of a thick yellow or green discharge from the vagina or penis and pain on urinating. It is spread by sexual contact. It was easily treated with the antibiotic penicillin until many resistant strains appeared. The spread can be controlled by treatment with antibiotics or the use of a barrier method of contraception such as a condom.

A fungal disease where purple or black spots develop on leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early. It affects the growth of the plant as photosynthesis is reduced. It is spread in the environment by water or wind, and can be treated by using fungicides and/or removing and destroying the affected leaves.
The pathogens that cause malaria are protists. Malaria causes recurrent episodes of fever and can be fatal.

An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another without being the pathogen itself. The malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito, so the spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.

concepts.term: non-specific defence systems of the human body
concepts.def: Defences that act against pathogens in general rather than one particular pathogen: the skin acts as a barrier; the nose has hairs and mucus that trap particles from the air; the trachea and bronchi produce mucus that traps pathogens and have cilia that waft the mucus away from the lungs; the stomach produces hydrochloric acid that kills pathogens in swallowed food and mucus.
The body system that tries to destroy a pathogen if that pathogen enters the body, after the non-specific defences have been passed.
One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: the white blood cell takes the pathogen into itself and digests it.

One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: white blood cells produce antibodies against the pathogen. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies.
One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: white blood cells produce antitoxins, which counteract the toxins produced by bacteria.

Introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies, preventing infection.

concepts.term: immunising a large proportion of the population
concepts.def: Vaccinating a large proportion of a population reduces the spread of a pathogen, because there are far fewer people the pathogen can infect and pass through.

A medicine, such as penicillin, that helps to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body. It is important that specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics. Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens.

A strain of bacteria that is not killed by an antibiotic. The use of antibiotics has greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases, but the emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern.

Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms. The heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves. The painkiller aspirin originates from willow. Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould.
The three things for which new drugs are extensively tested: toxicity, which is how harmful the drug is; efficacy, which is how well it works; and dose, which is how much of it should be given.
The stage of drug development done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals, before the drug is given to people.

The stage of drug development that uses healthy volunteers and patients. Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial. If the drug is found to be safe, further clinical trials are carried out to find the optimum dose for the drug. In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo.

options: A bacterium that causes an infectious disease
A poison that damages tissues and makes us ill
A microorganism that lives inside the body cells
A microorganism that causes infectious disease
mcqs.explain: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. They may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi, and may infect plants or animals.

mcqs.q: Purple and black spots have appeared on the leaves of a rose bush in a garden. How is this disease most likely to reach the other rose bushes in the garden?
options: By insects moving between the plants
By direct contact between the leaves
By toxins spreading through the soil
By water or wind in the environment
mcqs.explain: Rose black spot is a fungal disease that is spread in the environment by water or wind, so it can cross the gap between plants that never touch.

mcqs.q: What kind of pathogen causes malaria?
options: A protist spread to humans by mosquitos
A bacterium spread to humans by mosquitos
A mosquito that bites and infects humans
A virus that reproduces in human cells
mcqs.explain: The pathogens that cause malaria are protists, and the malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito.

mcqs.q: A health agency wants to reduce the number of malaria cases in a region. Which approach should it use?
options: Treating infected people with antibiotics
Stopping mosquitos breeding and using nets
Vaccinating whole populations against it
Avoiding direct contact with infected people
mcqs.explain: The spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.

mcqs.q: How is the spread of salmonella food poisoning controlled in the UK?
options: People are vaccinated against salmonella
Poultry are vaccinated against salmonella
Poultry are treated with strong antibiotics
People are given painkillers to cure it
mcqs.explain: Salmonella food poisoning is spread by bacteria ingested in food, and in the UK poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a non-specific defence system of the human body?
options: The nose produces antibodies to attack pathogens
The stomach produces acid that kills pathogens
Cilia in the trachea destroy trapped pathogens
White blood cells in the skin trap pathogens
mcqs.explain: The stomach is one of the non-specific defence systems of the human body: it produces hydrochloric acid that kills pathogens in swallowed food and mucus.

mcqs.q: Bacteria in the blood are releasing toxins. Which action of the white blood cells deals with those toxins?
options: The production of antibodies
The engulfing of the bacteria
The production of antitoxins
The production of stomach acid
mcqs.explain: White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by antitoxin production, and antitoxins counteract the toxins that bacteria produce.

mcqs.q: A pathogen gets past the body's non-specific defences and enters the body for the first time. What does the immune system do?
options: It produces toxins to kill the pathogen
It tries to destroy the invading pathogen
It develops resistance to the pathogen
It waits for a vaccination to be given
mcqs.explain: If a pathogen enters the body the immune system tries to destroy the pathogen, using phagocytosis, antibody production and antitoxin production.

mcqs.q: What is introduced into the body during a vaccination?
options: Dead or inactive forms of a pathogen
Ready-made antibodies from donors
Live and active forms of a pathogen
An antibiotic that kills pathogens
mcqs.explain: Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies.

mcqs.q: A large proportion of the population in a town is vaccinated against measles. What is the effect on the people in that town who are not vaccinated?
options: They are equally likely to catch measles
They are made immune to measles as well
They are less likely to catch measles
They must be given antibiotics instead
mcqs.explain: The spread of pathogens can be reduced by immunising a large proportion of the population, so an unvaccinated person is less likely to meet the measles virus.

mcqs.q: A patient has a viral infection and a painful sore throat. Which treatment is appropriate, and why?
options: Antibiotics, which kill the pathogen
Painkillers, which destroy the virus
Painkillers, which treat the symptoms
Antitoxins, which kill the pathogen
mcqs.explain: Painkillers and other medicines are used to treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens, so they are the appropriate treatment for the pain of a viral infection.

mcqs.q: The use of antibiotics greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases, but some bacterial infections are now much harder to treat. Why?
options: Patients have grown resistant to antibiotics
Antibiotics have started to kill viruses too
Bacteria now reproduce inside human cells
Resistant strains of bacteria have emerged
mcqs.explain: The emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern, because those strains are not killed by the antibiotic that once cured the disease.

mcqs.q: Why is it difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses?
options: Viruses live in cells, so tissues are damaged
Viruses reproduce outside the body's cells
Viruses make toxins that destroy the drugs
Viruses are easily destroyed by antibiotics
mcqs.explain: Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, so it is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues.

mcqs.q: A pharmaceutical company has synthesised a possible new drug. Which describes the preclinical testing of that drug?
options: Testing on healthy volunteers, patients
Testing on cells, tissues and live animals
Testing on patients at the optimum dose
Testing on some patients given a placebo
mcqs.explain: Preclinical testing is done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals, before the drug is given to any person.

mcqs.q: What happens in a double blind trial?
options: Some patients get a smaller dose
Healthy volunteers are in the trial
Some patients are given a placebo
Each patient gets the optimum dose
mcqs.explain: In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo rather than the drug being tested.

mcqs.q: Which drug is correctly matched with the source it originally came from?
options: Aspirin is extracted from foxgloves
Penicillin is extracted from foxgloves
Digitalis is extracted from foxgloves
Digitalis is extracted from the willow
mcqs.explain: Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms, and the heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves.

mcqs.q: Why must new medical drugs be tested and trialled before they are used?
options: To check they are safe and effective
To check they kill bacterial pathogens
To check they remove painful symptoms
To check patients cannot resist drugs
mcqs.explain: New medical drugs have to be tested and trialled before being used to check that they are safe and effective, which is why they are extensively tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose.

mcqs.q: How are most new drugs produced today?
options: Extracted from plants and microorganisms
Extracted from the willow and foxgloves
Collected from moulds growing in soil
Synthesised by pharmaceutical chemists
mcqs.explain: Most new drugs are synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry, although the starting point may still be a chemical extracted from a plant.
